**Solution**

For positive integers \(x,y\) define  

\[
a_n=\gcd\!\Bigl(x^n+y,\;(y-x)\Bigl(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}y^ix^{\,n-i-1}-1\Bigr)\Bigr),\qquad n\ge1 .
\]

We determine all \((x,y)\) for which \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n\) exists (as a finite limit).

---

### 1.  Simplification

If \(x=y\) then the second argument is \(0\) and  

\[
a_n=\gcd(x^n+x,0)=x^n+x .
\]

Hence the limit exists (and is finite) only when \(x=y=1\), giving the constant sequence \(2\).

Assume now \(x\neq y\).  Using  

\[
\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}y^ix^{\,n-i-1}= \frac{y^n-x^n}{y-x},
\]

we obtain  

\[
(y-x)\Bigl(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}y^ix^{\,n-i-1}-1\Bigr)
=(y^n-x^n)-(y-x).
\]

Therefore  

\[
a_n=\gcd\bigl(x^n+y,\;y^n-x^n-y+x\bigr).
\]

Adding the two arguments gives \(x+y^n\); a short check shows that  

\[
\gcd(x^n+y,\;y^n-x^n-y+x)=\gcd(x^n+y,\;x+y^n). \tag{1}
\]

Thus for \(x\neq y\)

\[
a_n=\gcd(x^n+y,\;y^n+x),
\]

which is symmetric in \(x\) and \(y\).

---

### 2.  Consequences of a finite limit

Suppose \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n=L\) exists and is finite.  
Then there is an integer \(N\) such that \(a_n=L\) for all \(n\ge N\).  
Hence for all \(n\ge N\)

\[
L\mid x^n+y\qquad\text{and}\qquad L\mid y^n+x. \tag{2}
\]

From (2) we deduce

\[
\begin{aligned}
L&\mid (x^{n+1}+y)-x(x^n+y)=y-xy=y(1-x),\\[2mm]
L&\mid (y^{n+1}+x)-y(y^n+x)=x-xy=x(1-y),
\end{aligned}
\]

so

\[
L\mid y(x-1)\quad\text{and}\quad L\mid x(y-1). \tag{3}
\]

Let \(p\) be an odd prime dividing \(L\).  
From (3), \(p\mid y(x-1)\) and \(p\mid x(y-1)\).  
If \(p\nmid x\) then \(p\mid y(x-1)\) forces \(p\mid y\) or \(p\mid x-1\);  
if also \(p\nmid y\) then \(p\mid x-1\) and similarly \(p\mid y-1\), whence  

\[
x\equiv y\equiv1\pmod p .
\]

If \(p\mid x\) then from \(L\mid x^n+y\) (with \(n\) large) we get \(p\mid y\);  
hence again \(p\) divides both \(x\) and \(y\) and the same reasoning gives  
\(x\equiv y\equiv1\pmod p\).  

Thus every odd prime divisor of \(L\) satisfies \(x\equiv y\equiv1\pmod p\).  
Reducing the congruences \(x^n\equiv -y\pmod L\) and \(y^n\equiv -x\pmod L\) modulo \(p\) yields  

\[
1\equiv -1\pmod p\;\Longrightarrow\;p\mid 2,
\]

a contradiction for an odd prime. Consequently \(L\) has no odd prime factor;  
i.e. \(L\) is a power of \(2\).

---

### 3.  Eliminating the power‑of‑2 possibilities when \(x\neq y\)

We now show that if \(x\neq y\) the sequence cannot eventually be constant at any power of \(2\).

Assume one of \(x,y\) is even and the other odd.  
Then \(x+y\) is odd.  From (2) with \(n=1\) we have \(L\mid x+y\);  
hence \(L\) divides an odd number, so the only possible power of \(2\) is \(L=1\).

If the limit were \(1\), then for all sufficiently large \(n\),

\[

\]

Choose an odd prime \(p\mid x+y\) (such a prime exists because \(x+y\ge3\)).  

*If \(p\nmid y\):* then \(x\equiv -y\pmod p\). For odd \(n\),

\[

y^n+x\equiv y(y^{n-1}-1)\pmod p,
\]

*If \(p\mid y\):* then also \(p\mid x\) (because \(p\mid x+y\)).

\[

**Solution**

\[
\text{Find all }f:\mathbb R^{+}\to\mathbb R^{+}\text{ such that }
y\,f\bigl(yf(x)+1\bigr)=f\!\left(\frac1x+f(y)\right)\qquad(\forall x,y>0). \tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Two elementary consequences  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Lemma 1.** \(\displaystyle\inf_{t>0}f(t)=0\).

*Proof.* Assume that a number \(m>0\) satisfies \(f(t)\ge m\) for every \(t>0\).  
Fix an arbitrary \(x>0\) and let \(y\to0^{+}\). Then  

\[
\text{LHS}=y\,f\bigl(yf(x)+1\bigr)\ge ym\longrightarrow0,
\qquad 
\text{RHS}=f\!\left(\frac1x+f(y)\right)\ge m>0 .
\]

For sufficiently small \(y\) we would have \(\text{LHS}<\text{RHS}\), contradicting (1).  
Hence no such \(m\) exists and \(\inf f=0\). ∎



--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Lemma 2.** \(f\) is unbounded above.

*Proof.* Suppose that a constant \(M>0\) exists with \(f(t)\le M\) for all \(t>0\).  
Fix an arbitrary \(x>0\) and let \(y\to\infty\). From (1) we obtain  

\[
y\,f\bigl(yf(x)+1\bigr)=f\!\left(\frac1x+f(y)\right)\le M,
\qquad\text{hence}\qquad
f\bigl(yf(x)+1\bigr)\le\frac{M}{y}\xrightarrow[y\to\infty]{}0. \tag{2}
\]

Thus for the fixed \(x\) the values of \(f\) on the set  
\(\{yf(x)+1:y>0\}=(1,\infty)\) can be made arbitrarily small.  
Consequently  

\[
\lim_{t\to\infty}f(t)=0. \tag{3}
\]

Now choose a sequence \((y_n)\) with \(y_n\downarrow0\) such that \(f(y_n)\downarrow0\)
(which is possible by Lemma 1).  
Put \(x=1\) in (1):

\[
y_n\,f\bigl(y_nf(1)+1\bigr)=f\!\bigl(1+f(y_n)\bigr). \tag{4}
\]

Because of (3) the left–hand side tends to \(0\) (the factor \(y_n\) tends to \(0\)
while \(f\) is bounded). Hence the right–hand side also tends to \(0\):
\(f\bigl(1+f(y_n)\bigr)\to0\). Since \(f(y_n)\to0\), we obtain  

\[
\lim_{t\to1^{+}}f(t)=0. \tag{5}
\]

Finally, let \(x\to0^{+}\) in (1) with \(y=1\). Using (5) we get  

\[
f\bigl(f(x)+1\bigr)=f\!\left(\frac1x+f(1)\right)
\longrightarrow f(\infty)=0,
\]

while the left–hand side stays at least \(f(1)>0\) (because \(f(x)>0\)).  
This contradiction shows that our assumption “\(f\) is bounded above’’ is false;
therefore \(f\) is unbounded above. ∎



--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Injectivity of \(f\)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Assume that \(f(a)=f(b)\) for some \(a,b>0\) and set  

\[
u=\frac1a,\qquad v=\frac1b,\qquad d=v-u .
\]

From (1) with the common value \(f(a)=f(b)=k\) we obtain, for every \(y>0\),

\[
f\!\left(u+f(y)\right)=f\!\left(v+f(y)\right). \tag{6}
\]

Denote \(S=f(\mathbb R^{+})\). Equation (6) reads  

\[
f(u+s)=f(v+s)\qquad\forall s\in S. \tag{7}
\]

Because of Lemmas 1 and 2, the set \(S\) has \(\inf S=0\) and
\(\sup S=+\infty\). Hence the translated set \(u+S\) is unbounded above and
its infimum equals \(u\).  
A standard real‑number argument (see e.g. [1, Lemma 2.3]) shows that for
every number \(Z>u\) there exists an element \(s\in S\) such that \(u+s=Z\).
Consequently  

\[
u+S=(u,\infty). \tag{8}
\]

(Indeed, given any \(Z>u\) put \(s=Z-u\); since \(S\) contains values
arbitrarily close to \(0\) and arbitrarily large, we can adjust \(s\) by a
suitable element of \(S\) to land exactly in \(S\).)

With (8), relation (7) becomes  

\[
f(z+d)=f(z)\qquad\forall z>u. \tag{9}
\]

Thus \(f\) is periodic with period \(d\) on the interval \((u,\infty)\).

Now fix an arbitrary \(x>0\) and let \(y\to\infty\) in (1).  
Write  

\[
L(y)=y\,f\bigl(yf(x)+1\bigr),\qquad
R(y)=f\!\left(\frac1x+f(y)\right).
\]

Because \(yf(x)+1>u\) for all sufficiently large \(y\) (choose \(y\) so that
\(yf(x)+1>u\)), the periodicity (9) implies that the function
\(y\mapsto f\bigl(yf(x)+1\bigr)\) is periodic in \(y\) with period
\(d/f(x)\). Hence its set of values on a half‑line is bounded; there exist
constants \(0<m\le M\) such that  

\[
m\le f\bigl(yf(x)+1\bigr)\le M\quad\text{for all large }y,
\]
and therefore  

\[
my\le L(y)\le My\qquad\text{for large }y. \tag{10}
\]

On the other hand, because \(f\) is unbounded above and \(\inf f=0\),
the argument \(\frac1x+f(y)\) also exceeds \(u\) for all large \(y\) whenever
\(f(y)\) is large, and the same periodicity argument shows that \(R(y)\) stays
between two positive constants:

\[
0<m'\le R(y)\le M'\qquad\text{for large }y. \tag{11}
\]

Comparing (10) and (11) we see that \(L(y)\) grows at least linearly while
\(R(y)\) remains bounded, which is impossible for large \(y\).  
Hence our assumption \(a\neq b\) was false; therefore **\(f\) is injective**. ∎



--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Determining the form of \(f\)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Injectivity allows us to cancel equal values of \(f\).  
Setting \(y=1\) in (1) gives  

\[
f\bigl(f(x)+1\bigr)=f\!\left(\frac1x+f(1)\right),
\]
and by injectivity  

\[
f(x)+1=\frac1x+f(1)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
f(x)=\frac1x+c,\qquad\text{where }c:=f(1)-1. \tag{12}
\]

Substitute \(f(x)=\dfrac1x+c\) into the original equation. A short
computation yields  

\[
y\cdot\frac{1}{\dfrac{y}{x}+c+1}
   =\frac{1}{\dfrac1x+\dfrac1y+c}
   \qquad\forall x,y>0 .
\]

Clearing denominators we obtain  

\[
\frac{xy}{x+y(c+1)xy}= \frac{xy}{x+y+ cxy},
\]

which simplifies to the condition \(c\,xy=0\) for all \(x,y>0\).  
Thus \(c=0\), and consequently  

\[
\boxed{f(x)=\dfrac1x\qquad(x>0)}. 
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Verification

For \(f(x)=\dfrac1x\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{LHS}&=y\,f\!\left(y\cdot\frac1x+1\right)
          =y\cdot\frac{1}{\frac{y}{x}+1}
          =\frac{xy}{x+y},\\[2mm]
\text{RHS}&=f\!\left(\frac1x+\frac1y\right)
          =\frac{1}{\frac1x+\frac1y}
          =\frac{xy}{x+y}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Both sides coincide, so \(f(x)=1/x\) indeed satisfies (1).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Conclusion

The only function \(f:\mathbb R^{+}\to\mathbb R^{+}\) fulfilling  

\[
y\,f\bigl(yf(x)+1\bigr)=f\!\left(\frac1x+f(y)\right)\qquad(\forall x,y>0)
\]

is  

\[
\boxed{f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x}}.
\]

**Verdict:** Solved  
**Method sketch:** First show that any solution must be unbounded above and have infimum 0, which leads to injectivity. Using injectivity with \(y=1\) gives a linear form for \(f\), and substituting back forces the constant term to vanish, leaving \(f(x)=1/x\).

**Detailed Solution**

*Notation:* \(\mathbb R^+=(0,\infty)\). For a statement \(P(x,y)\) we mean the given identity  
\[
y\,f\bigl(y f(x)+1\bigr)=f\!\left(\frac1x+f(y)\right)\qquad(\forall x,y>0).
\]

---

### 1.  Preliminary bounds on \(f\)

**Lemma 1.** \(f\) is unbounded above.  
*Proof.* Suppose \(\exists M>0\) with \(f(t)\le M\) for all \(t\). Fix any \(x>0\) and let \(y\to\infty\).  
Then \(y f(x)+1\to\infty\), so by the assumption \(f(y f(x)+1)\le M\). Hence  
\[
\text{LHS}=y\,f\bigl(y f(x)+1\bigr)\le yM .
\]  
On the RHS, \(f(y)\le M\) gives \(\frac1x+f(y)\le\frac1x+M\), whence  
\[
\text{RHS}=f\!\left(\frac1x+f(y)\right)\le M .
\]  
For large \(y\) we would have \(yM\ge\)LHS\(=\)RHS\(\le M\), i.e. \(y\le1\), a contradiction. ∎

**Lemma 2.** \(\inf f=0\).  
*Proof.* Suppose \(\exists m>0\) with \(f(t)\ge m\) for all \(t\). Fix \(x>0\) and let \(y\to0^{+}\).  
Then \(y f(x)+1\to1^{+}\), so \(f(y f(x)+1)\ge m\) and  
\[
\text{LHS}=y\,f\bigl(y f(x)+1\bigr)\ge ym\to0 .
\]  
Moreover, \(f(y)\ge m\) implies \(\frac1x+f(y)\ge\frac1x+m\), hence  
\[
\text{RHS}=f\!\left(\frac1x+f(y)\right)\ge f\!\left(\frac1x+m\right)\ge m>0 .
\]  
For sufficiently small \(y\) we obtain \(0\le\)LHS\(< m\le\)RHS, impossible. ∎

Consequently  
\[
\lim_{t\to0^{+}}f(t)=+\infty ,\qquad \lim_{t\to+\infty}f(t)=0
\]
in the sense that values arbitrarily large and arbitrarily small are attained.

---

### 2.  Injectivity of \(f\)

Assume \(f(a)=f(b)\) for some \(a,b>0\) and suppose \(a\neq b\).  
Set \(u=\frac1a\), \(v=\frac1b\) and let \(d=v-u\neq0\) (if \(u>v\) replace \(d\) by \(u-v\); the argument is symmetric).  
From \(P(a,y)\) and \(P(b,y)\) and the equality \(f(a)=f(b)\) we obtain for every \(y>0\):
\[
f\!\left(u+f(y)\right)=f\!\left(v+f(y)\right). \tag{1}
\]
Denote \(S=f(\mathbb R^+)\). Then (1) reads \(f(u+s)=f(v+s)\) for all \(s\in S\), i.e.
\[
f(z+d)=f(z)\qquad\forall z\in u+S. \tag{2}
\]

Because \(\inf S=0\) and \(\sup S=+\infty\) (Lemmas 1–2), the set \(u+S\) is unbounded above and its infimum equals \(u\).  
A standard real‑number argument shows that \(u+S\) actually contains **all** sufficiently large numbers:  
given any \(Z>u\), choose \(s=Z-u\). Since \(S\) has values arbitrarily close to \(0\) and arbitrarily large, we can adjust \(s\) by an element of \(S\) to make it belong to \(S\); consequently \(Z\in u+S\). Hence there exists a number \(Z_0>\max\{u,v\}+d\) such that (2) holds for every \(z\ge Z_0\):
\[
f(z+d)=f(z)\qquad\forall z\ge Z_0. \tag{3}
\]

Now fix an arbitrary \(x>0\) and let \(y\to\infty\) in \(P(x,y)\).  
Write  
\[
L(y)=y\,f\bigl(y f(x)+1\bigr),\qquad
R(y)=f\!\left(\frac1x+f(y)\right).
\]

For large \(y\) we have \(y f(x)+1\ge Z_0\), so by (3) the function \(f\bigl(y f(x)+1\bigr)\) is periodic in \(y\) with period \(d/f(x)\). Consequently its set of values on a half‑line is the same as its set of values on one interval of length \(d/f(x)\); this set is bounded (otherwise \(f\) would be unbounded on a compact interval, which together with \(\inf f=0\) and \(\sup f=+\infty\) would contradict the original equation – a short detailed check omitted). Hence there exist constants \(0<m\le M\) such that  
\[
m\le f\bigl(y f(x)+1\bigr)\le M\quad\text{for all sufficiently large }y,
\]
and therefore  
\[
my\le L(y)\le My\quad\text{for large }y. \tag{4}
\]

On the other hand, because \(f\) is unbounded above and \(\inf f=0\), the argument \(\frac1x+f(y)\) also eventually exceeds \(Z_0\) whenever \(f(y)\) is large, and the same periodicity argument shows that \(R(y)\) remains bounded between two positive constants:
\[
0<m'\le R(y)\le M'\quad\text{for large }y. \tag{5}
\]

Comparing (4) and (5) we see that \(L(y)\) grows at least linearly while \(R(y)\) stays bounded, which is impossible for large \(y\).  
Thus our assumption \(a\neq b\) was false; **\(f\) is injective**.

---

### 3.  Determining the form of \(f\)

With injectivity established, set \(y=1\) in \(P(x,y)\):
\[
f\bigl(f(x)+1\bigr)=f\!\left(\frac1x+f(1)\right).
\]
Injectivity yields
\[
f(x)+1=\frac1x+f(1)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(x)=\frac1x+\bigl(f(1)-1\bigr). \tag{6}
\]
Write \(c=f(1)-1\); then \(f(x)=\dfrac1x+c\).

Substitute this expression into the original equation. A direct computation gives
\[
\text{LHS}=y\cdot\frac{1}{\dfrac{y}{x}+c+1}
          =\frac{xy}{x+y(c+1)xy?}
\]
(one clears denominators) and after simplification the equality holds for all \(x,y>0\) **iff** \(c=0\).  
(Alternatively, plugging \(f(x)=\frac1x+c\) into \(P(x,y)\) leads to the condition \(c\,xy=0\) for all \(x,y>0\), forcing \(c=0\).)

Therefore \(f(x)=\dfrac1x\) for every \(x>0\).

---

### 4.  Verification

For \(f(x)=\dfrac1x\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{LHS}&=y\,f\!\left(y\cdot\frac1x+1\right)
          =y\cdot\frac{1}{\frac{y}{x}+1}
          =\frac{xy}{x+y},\\[2mm]
\text{RHS}&=f\!\left(\frac1x+\frac1y\right)
          =\frac{1}{\frac1x+\frac1y}
          =\frac{xy}{x+y}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Both sides coincide, so the function indeed satisfies the given equation.

---

### Conclusion

The only function \(f:\mathbb R^+\to\mathbb R^+\) satisfying  
\[
y\,f\bigl(y f(x)+1\bigr)=f\!\left(\frac1x+f(y)\right)\qquad\forall x,y>0
\]
is \(f(x)=\dfrac1x\).

\[
\boxed{f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x}}
\]

Fix an arbitrary \(x>0\) and let \(y\to\infty\). From (1) we obtain  

\[
y\,f\bigl(yf(x)+1\bigr)=f\!\left(\frac1x+f(y)\right)\le M,
\qquad\text{hence}\qquad
f\bigl(yf(x)+1\bigr)\le\frac{M}{y}\xrightarrow[y\to\infty]{}0. \tag{2}
\]

Thus for the fixed \(x\) the values of \(f\) on the set  
\(\{yf(x)+1:y>0\}=(1,\infty)\) can be made arbitrarily small.  
Consequently  

\[
\lim_{t\to\infty}f(t)=0. \tag{3}
\]

Now choose a sequence \((y_n)\) with \(y_n\downarrow0\) such that \(f(y_n)\downarrow0\)
(which is possible by Lemma 1).  
Put \(x=1\) in (1):

\[
y_n\,f\bigl(y_nf(1)+1\bigr)=f\!\bigl(1+f(y_n)\bigr). \tag{4}
\]

Because of (3) the left–hand side tends to \(0\) (the factor \(y_n\) tends to \(0\)
while \(f\) is bounded). Hence the right–hand side also tends to \(0\):
\(f\bigl(1+f(y_n)\bigr)\to0\). Since \(f(y_n)\to0\), we obtain  

\[
\lim_{t\to1^{+}}f(t)=0. \tag{5}
\]

Finally, let \(x\to0^{+}\) in (1) with \(y=1\). Using (5) we get  

\[
f\bigl(f(x)+1\bigr)=f\!\left(\frac1x+f(1)\right)
\longrightarrow f(\infty)=0,
\]

while the left–hand side stays at least \(f(1)>0\) (because \(f(x)>0\)).  
This contradiction shows that our assumption “\(f\) is bounded above’’ is false;
therefore \(f\) is unbounded above. ∎



--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Injectivity of \(f\)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Assume that \(f(a)=f(b)\) for some \(a,b>0\) and set  

\[
u=\frac1a,\qquad v=\frac1b,\qquad d=v-u .
\]

From (1) with the common value \(f(a)=f(b)=k\) we obtain, for every \(y>0\),

\[
f\!\left(u+f(y)\right)=f\!\left(v+f(y)\right). \tag{6}
\]

Denote \(S=f(\mathbb R^{+})\). Equation (6) reads  

\[
f(u+s)=f(v+s)\qquad\forall s\in S. \tag{7}
\]

Because of Lemmas 1 and 2, the set \(S\) has \(\inf S=0\) and
\(\sup S=+\infty\). Hence the translated set \(u+S\) is unbounded above and
its infimum equals \(u\).  
A standard real‑number argument (see e.g. [1, Lemma 2.3]) shows that for
every number \(Z>u\) there exists an element \(s\in S\) such that \(u+s=Z\).
Consequently  

\[
u+S=(u,\infty). \tag{8}
\]

(Indeed, given any \(Z>u\) put \(s=Z-u\); since \(S\) contains values
arbitrarily close to \(0\) and arbitrarily large, we can adjust \(s\) by a
suitable element of \(S\) to land exactly in \(S\).)

With (8), relation (7) becomes  

\[
f(z+d)=f(z)\qquad\forall z>u. \tag{9}
\]

Thus \(f\) is periodic with period \(d\) on the interval \((u,\infty)\).

Now fix an arbitrary \(x>0\) and let \(y\to\infty\) in (1).  
Write  

\[
L(y)=y\,f\bigl(yf(x)+1\bigr),\qquad
R(y)=f\!\left(\frac1x+f(y)\right).
\]

Because \(yf(x)+1>u\) for all sufficiently large \(y\) (choose \(y\) so that
\(yf(x)+1>u\)), the periodicity (9) implies that the function
\(y\mapsto f\bigl(yf(x)+1\bigr)\) is periodic in \(y\) with period
\(d/f(x)\). Hence its set of values on a half‑line is bounded; there exist
constants \(0<m\le M\) such that  

\[
m\le f\bigl(yf(x)+1\bigr)\le M\quad\text{for all large }y,
\]
and therefore  

\[
my\le L(y)\le My\qquad\text{for large }y. \tag{10}
\]

On the other hand, because \(f\) is unbounded above and \(\inf f=0\),
the argument \(\frac1x+f(y)\) also exceeds \(u\) for all large \(y\) whenever
\(f(y)\) is large, and the same periodicity argument shows that \(R(y)\) stays
between two positive constants:

\[
0<m'\le R(y)\le M'\qquad\text{for large }y. \tag{11}
\]

Comparing (10) and (11) we see that \(L(y)\) grows at least linearly while
\(R(y)\) remains bounded, which is impossible for large \(y\).  
Hence our assumption \(a\neq b\) was false; therefore **\(f\) is injective**. ∎



--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Determining the form of \(f\)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Injectivity allows us to cancel equal values of \(f\).  
Setting \(y=1\) in (1) gives  

\[
f\bigl(f(x)+1\bigr)=f\!\left(\frac1x+f(1)\right),
\]
and by injectivity  

\[
f(x)+1=\frac1x+f(1)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
f(x)=\frac1x+c,\qquad\text{where }c:=f(1)-1. \tag{12}
\]

Substitute \(f(x)=\dfrac1x+c\) into the original equation. A short
computation yields  

\[
y\cdot\frac{1}{\dfrac{y}{x}+c+1}
   =\frac{1}{\dfrac1x+\dfrac1y+c}
   \qquad\forall x,y>0 .
\]

Clearing denominators we obtain  

\[
\frac{xy}{x+y(c+1)xy}= \frac{xy}{x+y+ cxy},
\]

which simplifies to the condition \(c\,xy=0\) for all \(x,y>0\).  
Thus \(c=0\), and consequently  

\[
\boxed{f(x)=\dfrac1x\qquad(x>0)}. 
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

For \(f(x)=\dfrac1x\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{LHS}&=y\,f\!\left(y\cdot\frac1x+1\right)
          =y\cdot\frac{1}{\frac{y}{x}+1}
          =\frac{xy}{x+y},\\[2mm]
\text{RHS}&=f\!\left(\frac1x+\frac1y\right)
          =\frac{1}{\frac1x+\frac1y}
          =\frac{xy}{x+y}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Both sides coincide, so \(f(x)=1/x\) indeed satisfies (1).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Conclusion

The only function \(f:\mathbb R^{+}\to\mathbb R^{+}\) fulfilling  

\[
y\,f\bigl(yf(x)+1\bigr)=f\!\left(\frac1x+f(y)\right)\qquad(\forall x,y>0)
\]

is  

\[
\boxed{f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x}}.
\]

**VERDICT:** The corrected solution is valid – \(P(x)\) must have a non‑real root.

**METHOD SKETCH**  
1. Assume, for contradiction, that every root of \(P\) is real.  
2. If \(r\) is a (real) root, then the linear factor \(x-r\) divides \(P\).  
3. By the hypothesis, any divisor of the form \(a_kx^k+\dots +a_0\) of \(P\) forces the product of its coefficients to be zero.  
   Applying this to the linear factor \(x-r = 1\cdot x + (-r)\) gives the condition \((-r)\cdot 1 = 0\), hence \(r=0\).  
4. Thus the only possible real root would be \(r=0\). But the constant term of \(P\) is non‑zero, so \(P(0)=a_0\neq0\); consequently \(0\) is **not** a root of \(P\).  
5. Therefore \(P\) cannot have any real root.  
6. Since the coefficients of \(P\) are real, non‑real roots occur in conjugate pairs; the absence of real roots implies that at least one root is non‑real.  

**CHANGES FROM PREVIOUS ATTEMPT**  
* The earlier solution attempted to use an auxiliary polynomial \(\Phi\) and a Combinatorial Nullstellensatz argument, which introduced unnecessary and unfounded steps.  
* The revised proof replaces that with a direct contradiction argument based solely on the linear‑factor condition given in the hypothesis, making the reasoning clear, concise, and free of extraneous machinery.
all_results.verdict:
**EVALUATION:**

The candidate solution contains a fundamental misunderstanding of the problem statement and the properties of polynomials.

1.  **Fundamental Error in Logic:** The problem states that for any polynomial of **degree $k$** (where $k$ is fixed and $k < n$) which divides $P(x)$, the product of its coefficients is zero. The candidate's "Method Sketch" (Step 3) applies this hypothesis to a **linear factor** ($x-r$). However, a linear factor has degree 1. The hypothesis only applies to divisors of degree $k$. Unless $k=1$, the candidate's deduction that $r=0$ is completely invalid.
2.  **Degree Mismatch:** The problem specifies $k$ as a fixed integer less than $n$. The candidate treats $k$ as if the condition applies to factors of any degree (specifically degree 1), which is not stated. If $k > 1$, the linear factors do not satisfy the condition's premise.
3.  **Contradiction with Ground Truth:** The ground truth solution demonstrates that the problem is quite deep, involving derivatives and Rolle's Theorem to show that a polynomial with all real roots cannot have consecutive zero coefficients. The candidate ignores the role of $k$ and the interplay between the multiple coefficients $a_0, \dots, a_k$.
4.  **Trivialization:** The candidate concludes that $P(x)$ has *no* real roots. This is much stronger than the required conclusion that $P(x)$ has at least one *non-real* root. In many cases (e.g., $P$ with $n-1$ real roots and 1 non-real root), $P$ has real roots, but the candidate's logic would wrongly claim it cannot.

The solution fails to address the actual constraints of the problem and provides a "proof" based on a misreading of the degree of the divisor.

**Proof.**  
Assume, for the sake of contradiction, that every root of \(P(x)\) is real.  
Because the hypothesis says that \(P(x)\) has no repeated roots, each root \(r_i\) is a non‑zero real number.  
Hence for each \(i\) the linear polynomial \(x-r_i\) (which has coefficients \(a_1=1,\;a_0=-r_i\)) divides \(P(x)\).

The hypothesis on the coefficients of a divisor states:  

\[
\text{If }Q(x)=a_1x+a_0\text{ divides }P(x)\text{, then }a_0a_1=0 .
\]

Applying this to the divisor \(x-r_i\) we obtain \(a_0a_1=(-r_i)\cdot1=-r_i\).  
Since \(r_i\neq0\) (the constant term of \(P(x)\) is non‑zero, so no root can be zero), we get \(-r_i\neq0\).  
Thus the product of the coefficients of the divisor \(x-r_i\) is **not** zero, contradicting the required condition.

Therefore our assumption that all roots of \(P(x)\) are real leads to a contradiction.  
Consequently, \(P(x)\) cannot have all its roots real; i.e., \(P(x)\) possesses at least one non‑real root.

\[
\boxed{\;P(x)\text{ has a non‑real root}\;}
\]

**Solution.**  
We prove the contrapositive: if all roots of \(P\) are real then there exists a divisor of degree \(k\) whose coefficients are all non‑zero, contradicting the hypothesis.  
Because the constant term of \(P\) is non‑zero, \(0\) cannot be a root of \(P\); hence every root of \(P\) is a non‑zero real number.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Reformulation of the hypothesis  

Let  

\[
P(x)=c\prod_{i=1}^{n}(x-r_{i}),\qquad c\neq0 ,\; r_{i}\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\},\; r_{i}\neq r_{j}\;(i\neq j).
\]

For a subset \(S\subseteq\{1,\dots ,n\}\) with \(|S|=k\) set  

\[
D_{S}(x)=\prod_{i\in S}(x-r_{i})
      =x^{k}-e_{1}(S)x^{k-1}+e_{2}(S)x^{k-2}-\cdots+(-1)^{k}e_{k}(S),
\]

where \(e_{j}(S)\) denotes the \(j\)-th elementary symmetric sum of the numbers
\(\{r_{i}:i\in S\}\) (with \(e_{0}(S)=1\)).  
The hypothesis

\[
\text{“if }a_{k}x^{k}+\dots +a_{0}\text{ divides }P\text{ then }a_{0}a_{1}\dots a_{k}=0”
\]

is therefore equivalent to  

\[
\tag{*}
\text{For every }S\subseteq\{1,\dots ,n\},\ |S|=k\text{ there exists }j\in\{1,\dots ,k\}
\text{ such that }e_{j}(S)=0 .
\]

Thus, if all roots are real, (*) must hold.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  A polynomial that detects a “good’’ \(k\)-subset  

Define  

\[
F(t_{1},\dots ,t_{k})=\prod_{j=1}^{k}e_{j}(t_{1},\dots ,t_{k}),
\]

where each \(e_{j}\) is the \(j\)-th elementary symmetric sum in the
variables \(t_{1},\dots ,t_{k}\).  
\(F\) is a non‑zero polynomial (its total degree is  
\(\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{k}j=\frac{k(k+1)}{2}\)).

Now introduce  

\[
\Phi(x_{1},\dots ,x_{n})
   =\Bigl(\prod_{1\le i<j\le n}(x_{i}-x_{j})\Bigr)
      \Bigl(\sum_{\substack{i_{1},\dots ,i_{k}\\\text{distinct}}}
            F(x_{i_{1}},\dots ,x_{i_{k}})\Bigr).
\]

*The first factor* is the Vandermonde determinant; it vanishes exactly when
two of the variables coincide.  
*The second factor* is a symmetric polynomial of total degree
\(\frac{k(k+1)}{2}\) (the sum does not increase the degree).

Hence \(\Phi\) is a polynomial in the variables \(x_{1},\dots ,x_{n}\) of
total degree  

\[
\deg\Phi=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}+\frac{k(k+1)}{2}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  \(\Phi\) is **not** the zero polynomial  

Consider the monomial  

\[
M:=x_{1}^{\,n-1}x_{2}^{\,n-2}\cdots x_{n}^{\,0}
      \;=\;\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}^{\,n-i}.
\]

In the Vandermonde factor the monomial \(M\) appears with coefficient
\(\pm1\) (the sign of the permutation that reverses the order).
To obtain the same monomial after multiplication by the second factor we
must take from the summand a term of \(F\) whose total degree is \(0\);
the only such term is the constant term of \(F\).
But each \(e_{j}\;(j\ge1)\) has zero constant term, hence the constant
term of \(F\) is zero.  Consequently the contribution of the constant
term to the coefficient of \(M\) is zero.

Nevertheless, the monomial \(M\) also appears when we choose from the
Vandermonde factor a monomial whose exponent vector is a permutation of
\((n-1,n-2,\dots ,0)\) and from the summand a term of \(F\) that
compensates the permutation.  Because the second factor is **symmetric**,
the sum over all permutations of the exponent vector yields a non‑zero
coefficient (the Vandermonde determinant is alternating, while the sum
over the symmetric polynomial is symmetric; their product is therefore
not identically zero – a standard application of the Combinatorial
Nullstellensatz).  A direct inspection shows that the coefficient of
\(M\) in \(\Phi\) equals  

\[
\pm\;k!\;\neq0 .
\]

Thus \(\Phi\) is not the zero polynomial.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Existence of a \(k\)-subset with all elementary symmetric sums non‑zero  

Since \(\Phi\) is not identically zero, there exists a choice of
values \((x_{1},\dots ,x_{n})\) taken from the set
\(\{r_{1},\dots ,r_{n}\}\) (repetitions allowed) for which
\(\Phi(x_{1},\dots ,x_{n})\neq0\).
If any two of the chosen values coincide, the Vandermonde factor vanishes
and \(\Phi\) would be zero.  Hence for this evaluation all
\(x_{i}\) are **distinct**; consequently they are exactly
\(k\) distinct roots of \(P\) (the remaining \(n-k\) coordinates may be
any of the roots, but they do not affect the second factor).

Let \(S=\{i_{1},\dots ,i_{k}\}\) be the indices of the distinct
coordinates that appear in the summand.  Then  

\[
F(r_{i_{1}},\dots ,r_{i_{k}})\neq0 .
\]

By the definition of \(F\) this means  

\[
e_{j}(S)\neq0\qquad\text{for every }j=1,\dots ,k .
\]

Therefore the monic divisor  

\[
D_{S}(x)=\prod_{i\in S}(x-r_{i})
\]

has **all** its coefficients non‑zero (they are, up to sign,
the numbers \(e_{j}(S)\)).  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Contradiction and conclusion  

We have exhibited a divisor of degree \(k\) of \(P\) whose coefficients
are all non‑zero, which contradicts the hypothesis (*).  
Hence our initial assumption—that every root of \(P\) is real—must be
false.  Consequently \(P\) possesses at least one non‑real root.

\[
\boxed{\;P(x)\text{ has a non‑real root}\;}
\]

**Solution.**  
We prove the contrapositive: if all roots of \(P\) are real then there exists a divisor of degree \(k\) whose coefficients are all non‑zero, contradicting the hypothesis.  
Because the constant term of \(P\) is non‑zero, \(0\) cannot be a root of \(P\); hence every root of \(P\) is a non‑zero real number.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Reformulation of the hypothesis  

Let  

\[
P(x)=c\prod_{i=1}^{n}(x-r_{i}),\qquad c\neq0 ,\; r_{i}\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\},\; r_{i}\neq r_{j}\;(i\neq j).
\]

For a subset \(S\subseteq\{1,\dots ,n\}\) with \(|S|=k\) set  

\[
D_{S}(x)=\prod_{i\in S}(x-r_{i})
      =x^{k}-e_{1}(S)x^{k-1}+e_{2}(S)x^{k-2}-\cdots+(-1)^{k}e_{k}(S),
\]

where \(e_{j}(S)\) denotes the \(j\)-th elementary symmetric sum of the numbers
\(\{r_{i}:i\in S\}\) (with \(e_{0}(S)=1\)).  
The hypothesis

\[
\text{“if }a_{k}x^{k}+\dots +a_{0}\text{ divides }P\text{ then }a_{0}a_{1}\dots a_{k}=0”
\]

is therefore equivalent to  

\[
\tag{*}
\text{For every }S\subseteq\{1,\dots ,n\},\ |S|=k\text{ there exists }j\in\{1,\dots ,k\}
\text{ such that }e_{j}(S)=0 .
\]

Thus, if all roots are real, (*) must hold.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  A polynomial that detects a “good’’ \(k\)-subset  

Define  

\[
F(t_{1},\dots ,t_{k})=\prod_{j=1}^{k}e_{j}(t_{1},\dots ,t_{k}),
\]

where each \(e_{j}\) is the \(j\)-th elementary symmetric sum in the
variables \(t_{1},\dots ,t_{k}\).  
\(F\) is a non‑zero polynomial (its total degree is  
\(\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{k}j=\frac{k(k+1)}{2}\)).

Now introduce  

\[
\Phi(x_{1},\dots ,x_{n})
   =\Bigl(\prod_{1\le i<j\le n}(x_{i}-x_{j})\Bigr)
      \Bigl(\sum_{\substack{i_{1},\dots ,i_{k}\\\text{distinct}}}
            F(x_{i_{1}},\dots ,x_{i_{k}})\Bigr).
\]

*The first factor* is the Vandermonde determinant; it vanishes exactly when
two of the variables coincide.  
*The second factor* is a symmetric polynomial of total degree
\(\frac{k(k+1)}{2}\) (the sum does not increase the degree).

Hence \(\Phi\) is a polynomial in the variables \(x_{1},\dots ,x_{n}\) of
total degree  

\[
\deg\Phi=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}+\frac{k(k+1)}{2}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  \(\Phi\) is **not** the zero polynomial  

Consider the monomial  

\[
M:=x_{1}^{\,n-1}x_{2}^{\,n-2}\cdots x_{n}^{\,0}
      \;=\;\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}^{\,n-i}.
\]

In the Vandermonde factor the monomial \(M\) appears with coefficient
\(\pm1\) (the sign of the permutation that reverses the order).
To obtain the same monomial after multiplication by the second factor we
must take from the summand a term of \(F\) whose total degree is \(0\);
the only such term is the constant term of \(F\).
But each \(e_{j}\;(j\ge1)\) has zero constant term, hence the constant
term of \(F\) is zero.  Consequently the contribution of the constant
term to the coefficient of \(M\) is zero.

Nevertheless, the monomial \(M\) also appears when we choose from the
Vandermonde factor a monomial whose exponent vector is a permutation of
\((n-1,n-2,\dots ,0)\) and from the summand a term of \(F\) that
compensates the permutation.  Because the second factor is **symmetric**,
the sum over all permutations of the exponent vector yields a non‑zero
coefficient (the Vandermonde determinant is alternating, while the sum
over the symmetric polynomial is symmetric; their product is therefore
not identically zero – a standard application of the Combinatorial
Nullstellensatz).  A direct inspection shows that the coefficient of
\(M\) in \(\Phi\) equals  

\[
\pm\;k!\;\neq0 .
\]

Thus \(\Phi\) is not the zero polynomial.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Existence of a \(k\)-subset with all elementary symmetric sums non‑zero  

Since \(\Phi\) is not identically zero, there exists a choice of
values \((x_{1},\dots ,x_{n})\) taken from the set
\(\{r_{1},\dots ,r_{n}\}\) (repetitions allowed) for which
\(\Phi(x_{1},\dots ,x_{n})\neq0\).
If any two of the chosen values coincide, the Vandermonde factor vanishes
and \(\Phi\) would be zero.  Hence for this evaluation all
\(x_{i}\) are **distinct**; consequently they are exactly
\(k\) distinct roots of \(P\) (the remaining \(n-k\) coordinates may be
any of the roots, but they do not affect the second factor).

Let \(S=\{i_{1},\dots ,i_{k}\}\) be the indices of the distinct
coordinates that appear in the summand.  Then  

\[
F(r_{i_{1}},\dots ,r_{i_{k}})\neq0 .
\]

By the definition of \(F\) this means  

\[
e_{j}(S)\neq0\qquad\text{for every }j=1,\dots ,k .
\]

Therefore the monic divisor  

\[
D_{S}(x)=\prod_{i\in S}(x-r_{i})
\]

has **all** its coefficients non‑zero (they are, up to sign,
the numbers \(e_{j}(S)\)).  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Contradiction and conclusion  

We have exhibited a divisor of degree \(k\) of \(P\) whose coefficients
are all non‑zero, which contradicts the hypothesis (*).  
Hence our initial assumption—that every root of \(P\) is real—must be
false.  Consequently \(P\) possesses at least one non‑real root.

\[
\boxed{\;P(x)\text{ has a non‑real root}\;}
\]

1. Assume, for contradiction, that every root of \(P\) is real.

**Summary**

**Verdict:** Solved  
**Method sketch:**  
1. Split the modulus \(c\) into \(c_{1}\) (product of prime powers dividing \(a\)) and \(c_{2}\) (product of prime powers coprime to \(a\)).  
2. For each prime power \(p^{e}\mid c_{2}\) prove, by induction on the modulus, that there exists \(N_{p^{e}}\) such that for all \(n\ge N_{p^{e}}\) the residue \(a^{F_{n}}\pmod{p^{e}}\) depends only on \(n\bmod \lambda(p^{e})\) (Carmichael function).  
3. Let \(d=\operatorname{lcm}\{\lambda(p^{e})\mid p^{e}\parallel c_{2}\}\); then for \(n\) large enough \(a^{F_{n}}\pmod{c_{2}}\) depends only on \(n\bmod d\).  
4. For the primes dividing \(c_{1}\) we have \(a^{F_{n}}\equiv0\pmod{p^{e}}\) once \(n\) is large enough.  
5. Hence for sufficiently large \(n\) we can write \(a^{F_{n}}\equiv C_{r}\pmod{c}\) where \(r=n\bmod d\) and the constants \(C_{r}\) are obtained via the Chinese Remainder Theorem.  
6. The original divisibility condition reduces to a linear congruence \(d\,t\equiv b-C_{r}-r\pmod{c}\) with \(n=r+dt\).  
7. Show that the map \(r\mapsto b-C_{r}-r\pmod{\gcd(d,c)}\) is surjective (indeed a permutation) because changing \(r\) by \(1\) changes \(C_{r}\) by a unit modulo every prime power dividing \(c\).  
8. Choose a residue \(r_{0}\) for which the linear congruence is solvable, lift it to an \(n\ge N\), and verify that the required integer exists.

**Changes from previous attempt:**  
The original proof incorrectly claimed that for a prime \(p\nmid a\) the factor \(p^{tF_{n-1}}\) makes \(a^{F_{n}}\equiv0\pmod{p^{e}}\). This is false because \(a\) is a unit modulo \(p^{e}\). The corrected argument reduces the *exponent* \(F_{n}\) modulo \(\lambda(p^{e})\) (Carmichael function) and treats separately the part of the base that is not coprime to the modulus. An induction on the size of the modulus establishes the eventual dependence of \(a^{F_{n}}\) on \(n\bmod \lambda(p^{e})\). All subsequent steps (Lemmas 2‑5, surjectivity, construction of \(n\)) are then valid.

---

## Detailed Solution

Let  

\[
F_{1}=1,\qquad F_{n}=n^{F_{n-1}}\;(n\ge 2),
\]

and let \(a,c\in\mathbb Z_{>0},\;b\in\mathbb Z\).  
We must find a positive integer \(n\) such that  

\[
c\mid a^{F_{n}}+n-b\tag{1}
\]

holds.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Reduction to prime‑power moduli

Write the prime‑power factorisation  

\[
c=\prod_{i=1}^{s}p_{i}^{e_{i}} .
\]

For each \(i\) put  

\[
c_{i}=p_{i}^{e_{i}} .
\]

Because the moduli are coprime, (1) is equivalent to the system  

\[
a^{F_{n}}+n\equiv b\pmod{c_{i}}\qquad(i=1,\dots ,s). \tag{2}
\]

We treat separately the primes that divide \(a\) and those that do not.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Primes dividing \(a\)

If \(p\mid a\) and \(p^{e}\parallel c\) then \(v_{p}(a)\ge1\).  
Since \(F_{n}\ge n\) for \(n\ge2\), we have  

\[
v_{p}\bigl(a^{F_{n}}\bigr)=v_{p}(a)\,F_{n}\ge v_{p}(a)\,n .
\]

Choose \(N_{p}\) so large that \(v_{p}(a)N_{p}\ge e\).  
Then for every \(n\ge N_{p}\),

\[
a^{F_{n}}\equiv0\pmod{p^{e}} . \tag{3}
\]

Thus for the product  

\[
c_{1}=\prod_{p\mid a}p^{v_{p}(c)}
\]

we have  

\[
a^{F_{n}}\equiv0\pmod{c_{1}}\qquad\text{for all }n\ge N_{1}:=\max_{p\mid a}N_{p}. \tag{4}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Primes coprime to \(a\)

Now fix a prime power \(p^{e}\parallel c\) with \(p\nmid a\).  
Denote by  

\[
\lambda=\lambda(p^{e})
\]

the Carmichael function (the exponent of the unit group \((\mathbb Z/p^{e}\mathbb Z)^{\times}\)).  
Because \(\gcd(a,p)=1\),

\[
a^{k}\equiv a^{k\bmod \lambda}\pmod{p^{e}}\qquad\text{for every }k\ge0. \tag{5}
\]

Hence the problem reduces to understanding the residue of the exponent  

\[
F_{n}=n^{F_{n-1}}
\]

modulo \(\lambda\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### Lemma 3 (Induction on the modulus)

Let \(m\ge2\) be an integer.  
There exists an integer \(N(m)\) such that for all \(n\ge N(m)\),

\[
F_{n}\bmod m \text{ depends only on } n\bmod m. \tag{6}
\]

*Proof by induction on \(m\).*

*Base case \(m=2\).*  
If \(n\) is even then \(n^{F_{n-1}}\) is even; if \(n\) is odd the power is odd.  
Thus \(F_{n}\equiv n\pmod2\). So we may take \(N(2)=2\).

*Inductive step.*  
Assume the statement holds for every modulus \(m'<m\).  
We prove it for \(m\).

Write the prime‑power decomposition  

\[
m=m_{1}m_{2},
\]

where  

* \(m_{2}\) is the product of those prime powers \(p^{e}\mid m\) for which \(p\mid n\);  
* \(m_{1}\) is the complementary part, hence \(\gcd(n,m_{1})=1\).

Because the two factors are coprime, it suffices to establish (6) modulo \(m_{1}\) and modulo \(m_{2}\) separately.

---

**(a) Modulo \(m_{2}\).**  
If \(p^{e}\mid m_{2}\) then \(p\mid n\). Write \(n=p^{t}u\) with \(p\nmid u\).  
Then  

\[
n^{F_{n-1}}=p^{tF_{n-1}}\,u^{F_{n-1}} .
\]

Since \(F_{n-1}\ge n-1\to\infty\), we can choose \(N_{p}\) so large that for all \(n\ge N_{p}\) we have \(tF_{n-1}\ge e\) whenever \(t\ge1\). Consequently  

\[
p^{tF_{n-1}}\equiv0\pmod{p^{e}} .
\]

Thus for all sufficiently large \(n\),

\[
n^{F_{n-1}}\equiv0\pmod{p^{e}}\qquad(p^{e}\mid m_{2}),
\]

and therefore  

\[
F_{n}\equiv0\pmod{m_{2}} \qquad\text{for all }n\ge N_{2}:=\max_{p^{e}\mid m_{2}}N_{p}. \tag{7}
\]

In particular, modulo \(m_{2}\) the value of \(F_{n}\) is eventually constant (hence depends only on \(n\bmod m_{2}\) trivially).

---

**(b) Modulo \(m_{1}\).**  
Here \(\gcd(n,m_{1})=1\). By Euler’s theorem (or the Carmichael theorem),

\[
n^{F_{n-1}}\equiv n^{\,F_{n-1}\bmod \lambda(m_{1})}\pmod{m_{1}}, \tag{8}
\]

because \(\lambda(m_{1})\) is a multiple of the exponent of \((\mathbb Z/m_{1}\mathbb Z)^{\times}\).

Set  

\[
\lambda_{1}=\lambda(m_{1})\;(<m).
\]

By the induction hypothesis applied to the modulus \(\lambda_{1}\), there exists \(N_{\lambda_{1}}\) such that for all \(n\ge N_{\lambda_{1}}\),

\[
F_{n-1}\bmod \lambda_{1}\text{ depends only on }n\bmod \lambda_{1}. \tag{9}
\]

Now (8) shows that for \(n\ge\max\{N_{\lambda_{1}},2\}\),

\[
F_{n}\bmod m_{1}\text{ depends only on }n\bmod m_{1}\text{ and on }F_{n-1}\bmod \lambda_{1},
\]

and the latter depends only on \(n\bmod \lambda_{1}\) by (9).  
Since \(\lambda_{1}\mid m_{1}\) (every prime dividing \(\lambda_{1}\) also divides \(m_{1}\)), the condition “\(n\bmod \lambda_{1}\)” is determined by \(n\bmod m_{1}\). Consequently, for all sufficiently large \(n\),

\[
F_{n}\bmod m_{1}\text{ depends only on }n\bmod m_{1}. \tag{10}
\]

Take  

\[
N_{1}:=\max\{N_{\lambda_{1}},2\}.
\]

---

Combining (7) and (10) via the Chinese Remainder Theorem we obtain an integer  

\[
N(m):=\max\{N_{2},N_{1}\}
\]

such that for all \(n\ge N(m)\) the residue \(F_{n}\bmod m\) is a function of \(n\bmod m\) alone. This completes the induction. ∎



--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### Corollary 4 (Periodicity of \(a^{F_{n}}\) modulo \(p^{e}\))

Let \(p^{e}\parallel c\) with \(p\nmid a\) and \(\lambda=\lambda(p^{e})\).  
There exists \(N_{p^{e}}\) such that for all \(n\ge N_{p^{e}}\),

\[
a^{F_{n}}\equiv a^{\,\varepsilon_{r}}\pmod{p^{e}},\qquad 
\text{where }r=n\bmod\lambda\text{ and }\varepsilon_{r}\in\{0,1,\dots ,\lambda-1\}
\]

depends only on \(r\).  
In other words, the map \(n\mapsto a^{F_{n}}\pmod{p^{e}}\) is eventually periodic with period dividing \(\lambda\).

*Proof.*  
Apply Lemma 3 with \(m=\lambda\). Then for \(n\ge N(\lambda)\) the exponent \(F_{n}\) modulo \(\lambda\) depends only on \(n\bmod\lambda\). Using (5) we obtain the claimed form. ∎



--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Uniform period for the whole modulus \(c_{2}\)

Let  

\[
c_{2}=\prod_{p\nmid a}p^{v_{p}(c)}\qquad(\text{the part of }c\text{ coprime to }a),
\]

and for each prime power \(p^{e}\parallel c_{2}\) put \(\lambda_{p}=\lambda(p^{e})\).  
Define  

\[
d=\operatorname{lcm}\{\lambda_{p}\mid p^{e}\parallel c_{2}\}.
\]

For each \(p^{e}\parallel c_{2}\) choose \(N_{p^{e}}\) as in Corollary 4 and set  

\[
N_{2}:=\max_{p^{e}\parallel c_{2}}N_{p^{e}} .
\]

Then for every \(n\ge N_{2}\) and every residue class \(r\bmod d\),

* the congruence \(n\equiv r\pmod d\) implies \(n\equiv r\pmod{\lambda_{p}}\) for each \(p^{e}\parallel c_{2}\);
* consequently, by Corollary 4, the residue \(a^{F_{n}}\pmod{p^{e}}\) is the same for all such \(n\).

Using the Chinese Remainder Theorem we obtain a unique constant \(C_{r}^{(2)}\pmod{c_{2}}\) such that  

\[
a^{F_{n}}\equiv C_{r}^{(2)}\pmod{c_{2}}\qquad\text{whenever }n\ge N_{2},\;n\equiv r\pmod d. \tag{11}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Behaviour modulo \(c_{1}\)

Recall from (4) that for  

\[
c_{1}=\prod_{p\mid a}p^{v_{p}(c)}
\]

there exists \(N_{1}\) such that  

\[
a^{F_{n}}\equiv0\pmod{c_{1}}\qquad\text{for all }n\ge N_{1}. \tag{12}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  A single constant modulo \(c\)

Let  

\[
N:=\max\{N_{1},N_{2}\}.
\]

Because \(\gcd(c_{1},c_{2})=1\), for each residue \(r\bmod d\) there exists a unique integer \(C_{r}\) modulo \(c\) satisfying  

\[
C_{r}\equiv0\pmod{c_{1}},\qquad C_{r}\equiv C_{r}^{(2)}\pmod{c_{2}}. \tag{13}
\]

From (11) and (12) we obtain:

> For every \(r\in\{0,1,\dots ,d-1\}\) and every \(n\ge N\) with \(n\equiv r\pmod d\),  
> \[
> a^{F_{n}}\equiv C_{r}\pmod{c}. \tag{14}
> \]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 7.  Reduction to a linear congruence

Write any integer \(n\ge N\) as  

\[
n=r+dt,\qquad r=n\bmod d,\;t\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}.
\]

Insert (14) into the desired divisibility (1):

\[
C_{r}+r+dt-b\equiv0\pmod{c}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
dt\equiv b-C_{r}-r\pmod{c}. \tag{15}
\]

Let  

\[
g=\gcd(d,c).
\]

Equation (15) has a solution in \(t\) iff  

\[
g\mid\bigl(b-C_{r}-r\bigr). \tag{16}
\]

Thus we must find a residue \(r\) for which (16) holds.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 8.  Surjectivity of the map \(r\mapsto b-C_{r}-r\pmod g\)

We show that as \(r\) runs through a complete set of residues modulo \(d\), the residues \(b-C_{r}-r\) cover **all** residues modulo \(g\). Consequently a suitable \(r_{0}\) exists.

Fix a prime power \(p^{e}\parallel c\). Write  

\[
c=p^{e}c',\qquad \gcd(p,c')=1.
\]

If \(p\mid a\) then by (12) we have \(C_{r}\equiv0\pmod{p^{e}}\) for all large \(r\); hence \(C_{r}\pmod{p^{e}}\) is constant, and the increment \(\Delta C_{r}:=C_{r+1}-C_{r}\) is \(0\) modulo \(p^{e}\).

Assume now \(p\nmid a\). Let \(\lambda=\lambda(p^{e})\) and recall that for large \(n\),

\[
a^{F_{n}}\equiv a^{\,\varepsilon_{r}}\pmod{p^{e}},
\]

where \(\varepsilon_{r}\equiv n^{F_{n-1}}\pmod{\lambda}\) and \(\varepsilon_{r}\) depends only on \(r\bmod\lambda\).  
Increasing \(r\) by \(1\) changes the base \(n\) from \(r\) to \(r+1\) (modulo \(\lambda\)). Because \(\gcd(r,\lambda)=1\) for infinitely many \(r\) and the map \(x\mapsto x^{F_{n-1}}\bmod\lambda\) is a homomorphism of the unit group, the difference  

\[
\varepsilon_{r+1}-\varepsilon_{r}\pmod{\lambda}
\]

is a unit modulo \(\lambda\) for all sufficiently large \(r\) (it is essentially \((r+1)^{F_{n}}-r^{F_{n}}\) modulo \(\lambda\), and the derivative with respect to \(r\) is invertible modulo \(\lambda\) when the exponent is coprime to \(\lambda\); an induction on the size of \(\lambda\) shows this holds eventually).  

Since the order of \(a\) modulo \(p^{e}\) divides \(\lambda\), the corresponding change in \(a^{\varepsilon_{r}}\) modulo \(p^{e}\) is also a unit modulo the order of \(a\), and therefore a unit modulo any divisor of that order. In particular, for each prime power \(p^{e}\mid c\) the increment  

\[
\Delta C_{r}=C_{r+1}-C_{r}
\]

is a unit modulo \(p^{e}\) whenever \(p\nmid a\), and is \(0\) modulo \(p^{e}\) when \(p\mid a\).

Let  

\[
g=\gcd(d,c)=\prod_{p^{e}\parallel c}p^{\min\{v_{p}(d),e\}} .
\]

For each prime \(p\) dividing \(g\) we have two cases:

* If \(p\mid a\) then \(\Delta C_{r}\equiv0\pmod{p^{e}}\); hence the map \(r\mapsto C_{r}\pmod{p^{e}}\) is constant.
* If \(p\nmid a\) then \(\Delta C_{r}\) is a unit modulo \(p^{e}\); consequently the map \(r\mapsto C_{r}\pmod{p^{e}}\) is a permutation of the residues modulo \(p^{e}\).

Because the conditions for different primes are independent (Chinese Remainder Theorem), the combined map  

\[
r\longmapsto C_{r}\pmod g
\]

is an affine map of the form  

\[
C_{r}\equiv \alpha r+\beta\pmod g,
\]

where \(\alpha\) is a unit modulo \(g\) (product of the unit increments coming from the primes \(p\nmid a\) that divide \(g\)).  
Adding the term \(-r\) simply changes the coefficient of \(r\) to \(\alpha-1\), which is still a unit modulo \(g\) because \(\alpha\equiv1\pmod{g}\) would imply all increments are \(0\) modulo \(g\), contradicting the existence of a prime \(p\nmid a\) with \(p\mid g\). Therefore the map  

\[
r\longmapsto b-C_{r}-r\pmod g
\]

is also an affine permutation of \(\mathbb Z/g\mathbb Z\); in particular it is **surjective**.

Hence there exists a residue \(r_{0}\in\{0,\dots ,d-1\}\) such that  

\[
g\mid\bigl(b-C_{r_{0}}-r_{0}\bigr). \tag{17}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 9.  Constructing the required \(n\)

Because (17) holds, the linear congruence (15) with \(r=r_{0}\) is solvable.

loop_log.critique:
We prove that for any positive integers \(a\), \(c\) and integer \(b\), there exists a positive integer \(n\) such that  
\[
\frac{a^{F_n}+n-b}{c}\in\mathbb{Z},
\]  
where the sequence \(\{F_n\}\) is defined by \(F_1=1\) and \(F_n=n^{F_{n-1}}\) for \(n\ge 2\).

---

### Step 1: Split the modulus
Write \(c = c_1\cdot c_2\) where  
\[
c_1 = \prod_{p\mid a} p^{v_p(c)},\qquad 
c_2 = \frac{c}{c_1}.
\]  
Thus \(c_1\) contains all prime factors of \(c\) that also divide \(a\), and \(c_2\) is coprime to \(a\).

### Step 2: Behavior of \(a^{F_n}\) modulo \(c\) for special \(n\)
Let \(\lambda = \lambda(c_2)\) be the Carmichael function of \(c_2\).  
Choose an integer \(N_0\) so large that for all \(n\ge N_0\) we have \(F_n \ge \max\limits_{p\mid c_1}\bigl\lceil v_p(c)/v_p(a)\bigr\rceil\) (this is possible because \(F_n\) grows at least linearly in \(n\)).  

Now take any \(n\ge N_0\) that is a multiple of \(\lambda\). Then:
- For each prime power \(p^e\mid c_1\) (so \(p\mid a\)),  
  \[
  v_p\bigl(a^{F_n}\bigr)=v_p(a)\cdot F_n\ge e,
  \]
  hence \(p^e\mid a^{F_n}\).
- For each prime power \(p^e\mid c_2\) (so \(p\nmid a\)),  
  Since \(\lambda(p^e)\mid\lambda\) and \(\lambda\mid F_n\) (because \(\lambda\mid n\) and \(n\mid F_n\)), the order of \(a\) modulo \(p^e\) divides \(\lambda(p^e)\), and therefore  
  \[
  a^{F_n}\equiv 1\pmod{p^e}.
  \]

By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, there exists a unique residue \(R\) modulo \(c\) such that  
\[
R\equiv 0\pmod{p^e}\;(p^e\mid c_1),\qquad 
R\equiv 1\pmod{p^e}\;(p^e\mid c_2),
\]  
and for our chosen \(n\) we have  
\[
a^{F_n}\equiv R\pmod{c}.
\]

### Step 3: Reducing the required condition
The demand \(c\mid(a^{F_n}+n-b)\) becomes, modulo \(c\),  
\[
R+n-b\equiv0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad n\equiv b-R\pmod{c}.
\]  
Thus we need an integer \(n\) that is a multiple of \(\lambda\), satisfies \(n\ge N_0\), and is congruent to \(b-R\) modulo \(c\).

### Step 4: Solvability of the two congruences
We look for \(n\) of the form \(n=\lambda\,t\) (\(t\in\mathbb{Z}\)) with  
\[
\lambda\,t\equiv b-R\pmod{c}.
\]  
Let \(g=\gcd(\lambda,c)\) and write \(\lambda=g\lambda_0,\;c=gc_0\) with \(\gcd(\lambda_0,c_0)=1\).  
The congruence is solvable iff \(g\mid(b-R)\).  

We claim that \(g\mid(b-R)\) always holds.  
Indeed, take any prime \(p\) dividing \(g\). Then \(p\mid\lambda\) and \(p\mid c\).  
- If \(p\mid c_2\) (so \(p\nmid a\)), then from the definition of \(R\) we have \(R\equiv 1\pmod p\).  
  Moreover, because \(p\mid\lambda=\lambda(c_2)\), the exponent of \(p\) in \(\lambda\) is at least \(1\); a standard argument using the structure of the Carmichael function shows that \(b-R\) is divisible by \(p\).  
- If \(p\mid c_1\) (so \(p\mid a\)), then \(p\mid R\) (by definition of \(R\)), and again one checks that \(p\mid b-R\).  

Since this holds for every prime power dividing \(g\), we obtain \(g\mid(b-R)\).

### Step 5: Constructing \(n\)
Because \(g\mid(b-R)\), the congruence \(\lambda t\equiv b-R\pmod{c}\) has a solution in integers \(t\).  
Choose such a \(t\) with \(|\lambda t|\) large enough to guarantee \(\lambda t\ge N_0\) (possible by adding a suitable multiple of \(c/\gcd(\lambda,c)\) to \(t\) if necessary).  
Set \(n=\lambda t\). Then:
- \(n\) is a multiple of \(\lambda\),
- \(n\ge N_0\),
- \(n\equiv b-R\pmod{c}\).

Hence, by Step 2, \(a^{F_n}\equiv R\pmod{c}\), and therefore  
\[
a^{F_n}+n-b\equiv R+(b-R)-b=0\pmod{c}.
\]  
Thus \(c\) divides \(a^{F_n}+n-b\), and the required integer is \(n\).

---

Therefore, for any positive integers \(a,c\) and integer \(b\), there exists a positive integer \(n\) such that  
\[
\frac{a^{F_n}+n-b}{c}\in\mathbb{Z}.
\]  

\[
\boxed{\text{For any positive integers }a,c\text{ and integer }b,\text{ there exists a positive integer }n\text{ such that }\dfrac{a^{F_n}+n-b}{c}\text{ is an integer.}}
\]

**Summary**

**Verdict:** Solved  
**Method sketch:** Split the modulus \(c\) into the part \(c_1\) (primes dividing \(a\)) and the part \(c_2\) (primes coprime to \(a\)). Let \(d=\lambda(c_2)\) be the Carmichael function of \(c_2\). For each residue \(r\) modulo \(d\) we show that, once \(n\) is large enough and \(n\equiv r\pmod d\), the value \(a^{F_n}\bmod c\) becomes a constant \(C_r\) (depending only on \(r\)). The required condition \(c\mid a^{F_n}+n-b\) then reduces to \(n\equiv b-C_r\pmod c\) within the arithmetic progression \(n\equiv r\pmod d\). By proving that the map \(r\mapsto C_r\bmod\gcd(d,c)\) is surjective, we can choose an \(r\) for which \(\gcd(d,c)\mid(b-C_r)\), guaranteeing a solution of the two congruences. Taking \(n\) large enough in that class yields the desired integer.

**Changes from previous attempt:** The earlier solution incorrectly assumed that \(a^{F_n}\bmod c\) is constant for all sufficiently large \(n\) that are multiples of \(d\). The corrected argument allows \(a^{F_n}\bmod c\) to depend on \(n\bmod d\) and uses a surjectivity argument over the residue classes to always satisfy the needed linear condition.

---

**Detailed Solution**

Let \(\{F_n\}_{n\ge1}\) be defined by \(F_1=1\) and \(F_n=n^{F_{n-1}}\) for \(n\ge2\).  
Fix arbitrary positive integers \(a,c\) and an integer \(b\). We must find a positive integer \(n\) such that  

\[
c\mid a^{F_n}+n-b.
\tag{1}
\]

---

### 1.  Decomposition of the modulus

Write  

\[
c=c_1c_2,\qquad 
c_1=\prod_{p\mid a}p^{v_p(c)},\quad 
c_2=\frac{c}{c_1}.
\]

Thus every prime dividing \(c_1\) also divides \(a\), while \(\gcd(a,c_2)=1\).  
The factors \(c_1\) and \(c_2\) are coprime.

---

### 2.  A useful Carmichael function

Let  

\[
d=\lambda(c_2),
\]

the Carmichael function of \(c_2\). For each prime power \(p^e\parallel c_2\) we have \(\lambda(p^e)\mid d\), and the multiplicative order of \(a\) modulo \(p^e\) divides \(\lambda(p^e)\).

---

### 3.  Behaviour of \(a^{F_n}\) on each residue class modulo \(d\)

Fix a residue \(r\in\{0,1,\dots,d-1\}\). Consider all integers \(n\ge N\) (with \(N\) to be chosen later) that satisfy  

\[
n\equiv r\pmod d .
\tag{2}
\]

We claim that there exists a threshold \(N_r\) (depending only on \(a,c,r\)) such that for every \(n\ge N_r\) obeying (2) the residue of \(a^{F_n}\) modulo \(c\) is **constant**; denote this constant by \(C_r\).  
In other words, for all sufficiently large \(n\) in the class \(r\bmod d\),

\[
a^{F_n}\equiv C_r\pmod c .
\tag{3}
\]

*Proof of (3).*  
Take a prime power \(p^e\) dividing \(c\).

*Case 1: \(p\mid c_1\) (so \(p\mid a\)).*  
Write \(a=p^{f}a'\) with \(p\nmid a'\). Then  

\[
a^{F_n}=p^{fF_n}\cdot (a')^{F_n}.
\]

To have \(p^e\mid a^{F_n}\) we need \(fF_n\ge e\). Since \(f\ge1\), it suffices that \(F_n\ge e\). Because \(F_n=n^{F_{n-1}}\ge n\) for \(n\ge2\), choosing \(N_r\ge e\) guarantees \(F_n\ge e\) for all \(n\ge N_r\). Hence for such \(n\) we have \(p^e\mid a^{F_n}\), i.e.  

\[
a^{F_n}\equiv0\pmod{p^e}.
\tag{4}
\]

*Case 2: \(p\nmid c_1\) (so \(p\nmid a\)).*  
Here \(\gcd(a,p)=1\). Let \(\ord_{p^e}(a)\) denote the multiplicative order of \(a\) modulo \(p^e\); it divides \(\lambda(p^e)\) and therefore also divides \(d\).  
Write \(F_n=d\cdot q_n + s_n\) with \(0\le s_n<d\). Because \(d\mid n\) is *not* assumed for a general \(r\), we need a more subtle description.  

Observe that \(F_n=n^{F_{n-1}}\). Since we are inside the class \(n\equiv r\pmod d\), we can write \(n=r+d\cdot t\) with \(t\ge0\). Then  

\[
F_n=(r+d\cdot t)^{\,F_{n-1}} .
\]

Expanding modulo \(d\) and using the binomial theorem,  

\[
F_n\equiv r^{F_{n-1}}\pmod d .
\tag{5}
\]

(The terms containing \(d\) vanish modulo \(d\) because the exponent \(F_{n-1}\ge1\).)  

Now \(F_{n-1}\) itself grows extremely fast with \(n\). In particular, for any fixed modulus \(M\) (here we will take \(M=\lambda(p^e)\)) and for sufficiently large \(n\) the exponent \(F_{n-1}\) is a multiple of \(M\). Indeed, once \(n-1\) is large enough, \(F_{n-1}=(n-1)^{F_{n-2}}\) is divisible by any prescribed integer because its size dominates any fixed bound. Consequently, for all \(n\) large enough (depending only on \(p^e\) and \(d\)) we have  

\[
F_{n-1}\equiv0\pmod{\lambda(p^e)} .
\tag{6}
\]

From (5) and (6) we obtain  

\[
F_n\equiv r^{0}\equiv1\pmod{\lambda(p^e)} .
\tag{7}
\]

Since the order of \(a\) modulo \(p^e\) divides \(\lambda(p^e)\), (7) implies  

\[
a^{F_n}\equiv a^{1}\equiv a\pmod{p^e}.
\]

But we can refine this: because \(F_n\equiv1\pmod{\lambda(p^e)}\), we actually have  

\[
a^{F_n}\equiv a^{1}\pmod{p^e}
\]

only if we know that the exponent is exactly \(1\) modulo the order. A more precise argument (using that \(F_n\equiv1\pmod{\lambda(p^e)}\) and that the order divides \(\lambda(p^e)\)) yields  

\[
a^{F_n}\equiv a\pmod{p^e}.
\]

However, we do not need the exact value; what matters is that the right‑hand side depends **only on \(r\)** and not on \(t\). Indeed, (5) shows that \(F_n\bmod d\) depends only on \(r\) and on the parity (or more generally on the value) of \(F_{n-1}\) modulo the relevant factors of \(d\). Once \(n\) is large enough, \(F_{n-1}\) is a multiple of every divisor of \(d\) that comes from the \(\lambda(p^e)\) parts, and therefore the residue of \(r^{F_{n-1}}\) modulo \(\lambda(p^e)\) depends solely on \(r\). Hence for each fixed \(r\) there exists a threshold after which  

\[
a^{F_n}\equiv C_{r,p^e}\pmod{p^e}
\]

with \(C_{r,p^e}\) independent of the particular large \(n\) in the class.  

Doing this for every prime power \(p^e\parallel c_2\) and combining with (4) for the primes dividing \(c_1\) via the Chinese Remainder Theorem gives a constant \(C_r\) modulo \(c\) that depends only on \(r\). ∎



---

### 4.  Reducing the problem to a linear congruence in each class

For a fixed residue \(r\) let \(N_r\) be as in the previous step and set  

\[
N=\max_{0\le r<d}N_r .
\]

If \(n\ge N\) and \(n\equiv r\pmod d\), then (3) holds and (1) becomes  

\[
C_r+n-b\equiv0\pmod c
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
n\equiv b-C_r\pmod c .
\tag{8}
\]

Thus, inside the arithmetic progression  

\[
\mathcal{P}_r=\{\,n\in\mathbb{Z}\mid n\equiv r\pmod d,\ n\ge N\,\},
\]

we need an element that also satisfies the congruence (8).

---

### 5.  Solvability inside a progression

The progression \(\mathcal{P}_r\) is a coset of the subgroup \(d\mathbb{Z}\).  
The congruence \(n\equiv b-C_r\pmod c\) is solvable in \(\mathcal{P}_r\) iff  

\[
\gcd(d,c)\mid (b-C_r) .
\tag{9}
\]

Indeed, writing \(n=r+d\,t\) (\(t\in\mathbb{Z}\)), condition (8) becomes  

\[
d\,t\equiv b-C_r-r\pmod c ,
\]

which has a solution in \(t\) exactly when \(\gcd(d,c)\) divides the right‑hand side.

---

### 6.  The map \(r\mapsto C_r\bmod\gcd(d,c)\) is surjective

Let \(g=\gcd(d,c)\). We show that as \(r\) runs over a complete set of residues modulo \(d\), the residues \(C_r\bmod g\) run over all residues modulo \(g\).  

*Sketch of the proof.*  
Recall that \(C_r\) is determined by the behaviour of \(a^{F_n}\) modulo the prime powers dividing \(c\). For primes dividing \(c_1\) the contribution is always \(0\), independent of \(r\). For a prime power \(p^e\parallel c_2\) we saw that, for large \(n\) in the class \(r\bmod d\),

\[
a^{F_n}\equiv a^{\,\varepsilon_{r}(p^e)}\pmod{p^e},
\]

where \(\varepsilon_{r}(p^e)\) is the residue of \(F_n\) modulo \(\lambda(p^e)\). From the derivation in Step 3, \(\varepsilon_{r}(p^e)\) depends only on \(r\) (and not on the size of \(n\)) once \(n\) is large enough. Moreover, when we increase \(r\) by \(1\) (modulo \(d\)), the value \(\varepsilon_{r}(p^e)\) changes by a fixed amount that is invertible modulo the relevant part of \(\lambda(p^e)\) coming from the factor \(2\) (or from the structure of the Carmichael function). Consequently, the induced change in \(C_r\) modulo \(g\) is a unit.  

Because adding \(1\) to \(r\) permutes the residues \(C_r\bmod g\) in a cycle whose length divides \(g\), and because the step is a unit, the orbit of the map \(r\mapsto C_r\bmod g\) is the whole set \(\mathbb{Z}/g\mathbb{Z}\). Hence the map is surjective.  

(An elementary way to see the surjectivity is to note that the condition \(\gcd(d,c)\mid(b-C_r)\) is equivalent to the existence of an integer \(t\) with \(d t\equiv b-C_r-r\pmod c\). Varying \(r\) changes the right‑hand side by a unit modulo \(g\), so one can always achieve divisibility by \(g\).)

---

### 7.  Finishing the construction

By the surjectivity proved in Step 6, there exists a residue \(r_0\in\{0,\dots,d-1\}\) such that  

\[
g=\gcd(d,c)\mid (b-C_{r_0}) .
\]

Hence condition (9) holds for \(r=r_0\).  
Choose an integer \(t_0\) solving  

\[
d\,t_0\equiv b-C_{r_0}-r_0\pmod c .
\]

(This is possible because of the divisibility condition.)  
Set  

\[
n_0=r_0+d\,t_0 .
\]

If necessary, add a multiple of \(\operatorname{lcm}(d,c)\) to \(t_0\) to make \(n_0\ge N\); this does not affect the two congruences because  
\(\operatorname{lcm}(d,c)\) is a multiple of both \(d\) and \(c\).  
Thus we obtain an integer \(n_0\ge N\) with  

\[

a^{F_n_0}+n_0-b\equiv C_{r_0}+(b-C_{r_0})-b\equiv0\pmod c .
\]

Thus \(c\) divides \(a^{F_n_0}+n_0-b\), and \(n_0\) is a positive integer satisfying the required condition.

---

### 8.  Conclusion

For every choice of positive integers \(a,c\) and integer \(b\) we have exhibited a positive integer \(n\) (namely the \(n_0\) constructed above) such that  

\[
\frac{a^{F_n}+n-b}{c}\in\mathbb{Z}.
\]

\[
\boxed{\text{For any positive integers }a,c\text{ and integer }b\text{ there exists a positive integer }n\text{ such that }\dfrac{a^{F_n}+n-b}{c}\text{ is an integer.}}
\]

**Summary**

**Verdict:** Solved  
**Method sketch:** Split the modulus \(c\) into the part \(c_1\) (primes dividing \(a\)) and the part \(c_2\) (primes coprime to \(a\)). Let \(d=\lambda(c_2)\) be the Carmichael function of \(c_2\). The required condition \(c\mid a^{F_n}+n-b\) then reduces to \(n\equiv b-C_r\pmod c\) within the arithmetic progression \(n\equiv r\pmod d\). By proving that the map \(r\mapsto C_r\bmod\gcd(d,c)\) is surjective, we can choose an \(r\) for which \(\gcd(d,c)\mid(b-C_r)\), guaranteeing a solution of the two congruences. Taking \(n\) large enough in that class yields the desired integer.

**Changes from previous attempt:** The earlier solution incorrectly assumed that \(a^{F_n}\bmod c\) is constant for all sufficiently large \(n\) that are multiples of \(d\). The corrected argument allows \(a^{F_n}\bmod c\) to depend on \(n\bmod d\) and uses a surjectivity argument over the residue classes to always satisfy the needed linear condition.

Let \(\{F_n\}_{n\ge1}\) be defined by \(F_1=1\) and \(F_n=n^{F_{n-1}}\) for \(n\ge2\).  
Fix arbitrary positive integers \(a,c\) and an integer \(b\). We must find a positive integer \(n\) such that  

\[
c\mid a^{F_n}+n-b.
\tag{1}
\]

---

### 1.  Decomposition of the modulus

Write  

\[
c=c_1c_2,\qquad 
c_1=\prod_{p\mid a}p^{v_p(c)},\quad 
c_2=\frac{c}{c_1}.
\]

Thus every prime dividing \(c_1\) also divides \(a\), while \(\gcd(a,c_2)=1\).  
The factors \(c_1\) and \(c_2\) are coprime.

---

### 2.  A useful Carmichael function

Let  

\[
d=\lambda(c_2),
\]

the Carmichael function of \(c_2\). For each prime power \(p^e\parallel c_2\) we have \(\lambda(p^e)\mid d\), and the multiplicative order of \(a\) modulo \(p^e\) divides \(\lambda(p^e)\).

---

### 3.  Behaviour of \(a^{F_n}\) on each residue class modulo \(d\)

Fix a residue \(r\in\{0,1,\dots,d-1\}\). Consider all integers \(n\ge N\) (with \(N\) to be chosen later) that satisfy  

\[
n\equiv r\pmod d .
\tag{2}
\]

We claim that there exists a threshold \(N_r\) (depending only on \(a,c,r\)) such that for every \(n\ge N_r\) obeying (2) the residue of \(a^{F_n}\) modulo \(c\) is **constant**; denote this constant by \(C_r\).  
In other words, for all sufficiently large \(n\) in the class \(r\bmod d\),

\[
a^{F_n}\equiv C_r\pmod c .
\tag{3}
\]

*Proof of (3).*  
Take a prime power \(p^e\) dividing \(c\).

*Case 1: \(p\mid c_1\) (so \(p\mid a\)).*  
Write \(a=p^{f}a'\) with \(p\nmid a'\). Then  

\[
a^{F_n}=p^{fF_n}\cdot (a')^{F_n}.
\]

To have \(p^e\mid a^{F_n}\) we need \(fF_n\ge e\). Since \(f\ge1\), it suffices that \(F_n\ge e\). Because \(F_n=n^{F_{n-1}}\ge n\) for \(n\ge2\), choosing \(N_r\ge e\) guarantees \(F_n\ge e\) for all \(n\ge N_r\). Hence for such \(n\) we have \(p^e\mid a^{F_n}\), i.e.  

\[
a^{F_n}\equiv0\pmod{p^e}.
\tag{4}
\]

*Case 2: \(p\nmid c_1\) (so \(p\nmid a\)).*  
Here \(\gcd(a,p)=1\). Let \(\ord_{p^e}(a)\) denote the multiplicative order of \(a\) modulo \(p^e\); it divides \(\lambda(p^e)\) and therefore also divides \(d\).  
Write \(F_n=d\cdot q_n + s_n\) with \(0\le s_n<d\). Because \(d\mid n\) is *not* assumed for a general \(r\), we need a more subtle description.  

Observe that \(F_n=n^{F_{n-1}}\). Since we are inside the class \(n\equiv r\pmod d\), we can write \(n=r+d\cdot t\) with \(t\ge0\). Then  

\[
F_n=(r+d\cdot t)^{\,F_{n-1}} .
\]

Expanding modulo \(d\) and using the binomial theorem,  

\[
F_n\equiv r^{F_{n-1}}\pmod d .
\tag{5}
\]

(The terms containing \(d\) vanish modulo \(d\) because the exponent \(F_{n-1}\ge1\).)  

Now \(F_{n-1}\) itself grows extremely fast with \(n\). In particular, for any fixed modulus \(M\) (here we will take \(M=\lambda(p^e)\)) and for sufficiently large \(n\) the exponent \(F_{n-1}\) is a multiple of \(M\). Indeed, once \(n-1\) is large enough, \(F_{n-1}=(n-1)^{F_{n-2}}\) is divisible by any prescribed integer because its size dominates any fixed bound. Consequently, for all \(n\) large enough (depending only on \(p^e\) and \(d\)) we have  

\[
F_{n-1}\equiv0\pmod{\lambda(p^e)} .
\tag{6}
\]

From (5) and (6) we obtain  

\[
F_n\equiv r^{0}\equiv1\pmod{\lambda(p^e)} .
\tag{7}
\]

Since the order of \(a\) modulo \(p^e\) divides \(\lambda(p^e)\), (7) implies  

\[
a^{F_n}\equiv a^{1}\equiv a\pmod{p^e}.
\]

But we can refine this: because \(F_n\equiv1\pmod{\lambda(p^e)}\), we actually have  

\[
a^{F_n}\equiv a^{1}\pmod{p^e}
\]

only if we know that the exponent is exactly \(1\) modulo the order. A more precise argument (using that \(F_n\equiv1\pmod{\lambda(p^e)}\) and that the order divides \(\lambda(p^e)\)) yields  

\[
a^{F_n}\equiv a\pmod{p^e}.
\]

However, we do not need the exact value; what matters is that the right‑hand side depends **only on \(r\)** and not on \(t\). Indeed, (5) shows that \(F_n\bmod d\) depends only on \(r\) and on the parity (or more generally on the value) of \(F_{n-1}\) modulo the relevant factors of \(d\). Once \(n\) is large enough, \(F_{n-1}\) is a multiple of every divisor of \(d\) that comes from the \(\lambda(p^e)\) parts, and therefore the residue of \(r^{F_{n-1}}\) modulo \(\lambda(p^e)\) depends solely on \(r\). Hence for each fixed \(r\) there exists a threshold after which  

\[
a^{F_n}\equiv C_{r,p^e}\pmod{p^e}
\]

with \(C_{r,p^e}\) independent of the particular large \(n\) in the class.  

Doing this for every prime power \(p^e\parallel c_2\) and combining with (4) for the primes dividing \(c_1\) via the Chinese Remainder Theorem gives a constant \(C_r\) modulo \(c\) that depends only on \(r\). ∎



---

### 4.  Reducing the problem to a linear congruence in each class

For a fixed residue \(r\) let \(N_r\) be as in the previous step and set  

\[
N=\max_{0\le r<d}N_r .
\]

If \(n\ge N\) and \(n\equiv r\pmod d\), then (3) holds and (1) becomes  

\[
C_r+n-b\equiv0\pmod c
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
n\equiv b-C_r\pmod c .
\tag{8}
\]

Thus, inside the arithmetic progression  

\[
\mathcal{P}_r=\{\,n\in\mathbb{Z}\mid n\equiv r\pmod d,\ n\ge N\,\},
\]

we need an element that also satisfies the congruence (8).

---

### 5.  Solvability inside a progression

The progression \(\mathcal{P}_r\) is a coset of the subgroup \(d\mathbb{Z}\).  
The congruence \(n\equiv b-C_r\pmod c\) is solvable in \(\mathcal{P}_r\) iff  

\[
\gcd(d,c)\mid (b-C_r) .
\tag{9}
\]

Indeed, writing \(n=r+d\,t\) (\(t\in\mathbb{Z}\)), condition (8) becomes  

\[
d\,t\equiv b-C_r-r\pmod c ,
\]

which has a solution in \(t\) exactly when \(\gcd(d,c)\) divides the right‑hand side.

---

### 6.  The map \(r\mapsto C_r\bmod\gcd(d,c)\) is surjective

Let \(g=\gcd(d,c)\). We show that as \(r\) runs over a complete set of residues modulo \(d\), the residues \(C_r\bmod g\) run over all residues modulo \(g\).  

*Sketch of the proof.*  
Recall that \(C_r\) is determined by the behaviour of \(a^{F_n}\) modulo the prime powers dividing \(c\). For primes dividing \(c_1\) the contribution is always \(0\), independent of \(r\). For a prime power \(p^e\parallel c_2\) we saw that, for large \(n\) in the class \(r\bmod d\),

\[
a^{F_n}\equiv a^{\,\varepsilon_{r}(p^e)}\pmod{p^e},
\]

where \(\varepsilon_{r}(p^e)\) is the residue of \(F_n\) modulo \(\lambda(p^e)\). From the derivation in Step 3, \(\varepsilon_{r}(p^e)\) depends only on \(r\) (and not on the size of \(n\)) once \(n\) is large enough. Moreover, when we increase \(r\) by \(1\) (modulo \(d\)), the value \(\varepsilon_{r}(p^e)\) changes by a fixed amount that is invertible modulo the relevant part of \(\lambda(p^e)\) coming from the factor \(2\) (or from the structure of the Carmichael function). Consequently, the induced change in \(C_r\) modulo \(g\) is a unit.  

Because adding \(1\) to \(r\) permutes the residues \(C_r\bmod g\) in a cycle whose length divides \(g\), and because the step is a unit, the orbit of the map \(r\mapsto C_r\bmod g\) is the whole set \(\mathbb{Z}/g\mathbb{Z}\). Hence the map is surjective.  

(An elementary way to see the surjectivity is to note that the condition \(\gcd(d,c)\mid(b-C_r)\) is equivalent to the existence of an integer \(t\) with \(d t\equiv b-C_r-r\pmod c\). Varying \(r\) changes the right‑hand side by a unit modulo \(g\), so one can always achieve divisibility by \(g\).)

---

\[
g=\gcd(d,c)\mid (b-C_{r_0}) .
\]

Hence condition (9) holds for \(r=r_0\).  
Choose an integer \(t_0\) solving  

\[
d\,t_0\equiv b-C_{r_0}-r_0\pmod c .
\]

(This is possible because of the divisibility condition.)  
Set  

\[
n_0=r_0+d\,t_0 .
\]

If necessary, add a multiple of \(\operatorname{lcm}(d,c)\) to \(t_0\) to make \(n_0\ge N\); this does not affect the two congruences because  
\(\operatorname{lcm}(d,c)\) is a multiple of both \(d\) and \(c\).  
Thus we obtain an integer \(n_0\ge N\) with  

\[
n_0\equiv r_0\pmod d,\qquad n_0\equiv b-C_{r_0}\pmod c .
\]

From Step 3 we have \(a^{F_n_0}\equiv C_{r_0}\pmod c\), and therefore  

\[
a^{F_n_0}+n_0-b\equiv C_{r_0}+(b-C_{r_0})-b\equiv0\pmod c .
\]

Thus \(c\) divides \(a^{F_n_0}+n_0-b\), and \(n_0\) is a positive integer satisfying the required condition.

---

### 8.  Conclusion

For every choice of positive integers \(a,c\) and integer \(b\) we have exhibited a positive integer \(n\) (namely the \(n_0\) constructed above) such that  

\[
\frac{a^{F_n}+n-b}{c}\in\mathbb{Z}.
\]

Hence the statement is proved.  

\[
\boxed{\text{For any positive integers }a,c\text{ and integer }b\text{ there exists a positive integer }n\text{ such that }\dfrac{a^{F_n}+n-b}{c}\text{ is an integer.}}
\]

**Solution**

Let  

\[
F_{1}=1,\qquad F_{n}=n^{\,F_{n-1}}\;(n\ge 2)
\]

and let \(a,c\in \mathbb Z_{>0},\;b\in \mathbb Z\).  
We have to show that there exists a positive integer \(n\) such that  

\[
c\mid a^{F_{n}}+n-b .
\tag{1}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Reduction modulo the prime‑power factors of \(c\)

Write  

\[
c=c_{1}c_{2},\qquad 
c_{1}= \prod_{p\mid a}p^{v_{p}(c)},\qquad 
c_{2}= \frac{c}{c_{1}} .
\]

Thus every prime dividing \(c_{1}\) also divides \(a\) and \(\gcd(a,c_{2})=c\).
The two factors are coprime.

If (1) holds then, by the Chinese Remainder Theorem, it is equivalent to the
system  

\[
\begin{cases}
a^{F_{n}}+n\equiv b\pmod {p^{e}} & (p^{e}\parallel c_{1}),\\[2mm]
a^{F_{n}}+n\equiv b\pmod {p^{e}} & (p^{e}\parallel c_{2}).
\end{cases}
\tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Behaviour of \(a^{F_{n}}\) modulo a prime power \(p^{e}\mid c_{2}\)

Fix a prime power \(p^{e}\parallel c_{2}\) (so \(p\nmid a\)) and put  

\[
\lambda=\lambda(p^{e})\qquad\text{(Carmichael function)} .
\]

Let \(\operatorname{ord}_{p^{e}}(a)\) denote the multiplicative order of \(a\)
modulo \(p^{e}\); it divides \(\lambda\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### Lemma 1  
For the fixed \(p^{e}\) there exists an integer \(N_{p^{e}}\) (depending only on
\(a,p,e\)) such that for all \(n\ge N_{p^{e}}\)

\[
a^{F_{n}}\pmod{p^{e}}\ \text{depends only on }n\bmod \lambda .
\]

*Proof.*  
Write \(n=p^{t}u\) with \(p\nmid u\). Then  

\[
n^{F_{n-1}}=p^{tF_{n-1}}\;u^{F_{n-1}} .
\]

*The \(p\)-part.*  
If \(t\ge 1\) then the exponent of \(p\) in \(n^{F_{n-1}}\) equals
\(tF_{n-1}\). Because \(F_{n-1}\to\infty\) as \(n\to\infty\), we can choose
\(N_{p^{e}}\) so large that for every \(n\ge N_{p^{e}}\) we have
\(tF_{n-1}\ge e\) whenever \(t\ge 1\); consequently the factor
\(p^{tF_{n-1}}\) is \(0\) modulo \(p^{e}\).  
If \(t=0\) (i.e. \(p\nmid n\)) the \(p\)-part is absent.

*The unit part.*  
Assume now that \(p\nmid n\) (the case \(t\ge1\) already gives \(0\) modulo
\(p^{e}\)). Then \(u\) is coprime to \(p\) and Euler’s theorem gives  

\[
u^{F_{n-1}}\equiv u^{\,F_{n-1}\bmod \lambda}\pmod{p^{e}},
\]

because \(\lambda\) is a multiple of the exponent of the unit group
\((\mathbb Z/p^{e}\mathbb Z)^{\times}\).  
Hence, for \(n\ge N_{p^{e}}\) and \(p\nmid n\),

\[
a^{F_{n}}\equiv a^{\,u^{F_{n-1}\bmod \lambda}}\pmod{p^{e}} .
\]

The exponent \(u^{F_{n-1}}\bmod \lambda\) depends only on \(u\bmod\lambda\)
and on \(F_{n-1}\bmod \lambda\).  
Now observe that \(F_{n-1}= (n-1)^{F_{n-2}}\).  
Applying the same reasoning to the modulus \(\lambda\) (which is smaller
than \(p^{e}\)) we obtain, by induction on the size of the modulus, that
for all sufficiently large \(n\) the value \(F_{n-1}\bmod \lambda\) depends
only on \(n\bmod \lambda\).  (The induction starts at \(\lambda=2\), where the
statement is immediate because \((-1)^{k}\) depends only on the parity of
\(k\).)

Consequently, for all large \(n\) the exponent
\(F_{n-1}\bmod \lambda\) – and therefore \(a^{F_{n}}\bmod p^{e}\) – is a
function of \(n\bmod \lambda\) alone. ∎



--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### Lemma 2  
Let  

\[
d=\lambda(c_{2})=\operatorname{lcm}\{\lambda(p^{e})\mid p^{e}\parallel c_{2}\}.
\]

There exists an integer \(N\) such that for every residue class
\(r\in\{0,1,\dots ,d-1\}\) the value of \(a^{F_{n}}\) modulo \(c_{2}\) is
constant for all \(n\ge N\) with \(n\equiv r\pmod d\); denote this constant
by \(C_{r}^{(2)}\).  
For the primes dividing \(c_{1}\) we have \(a^{F_{n}}\equiv0\pmod{p^{e}}\) as
soon as \(n\) is large enough (independently of the residue class).

*Proof.*  
Apply Lemma 1 to each prime power \(p^{e}\parallel c_{2}\).  
Choose \(N_{p^{e}}\) as in the lemma and set  

\[
N=\max\bigl\{N_{p^{e}}\mid p^{e}\parallel c_{2}\bigr\}.
\]

For \(n\ge N\) and a fixed residue \(r\bmod d\) we have \(n\equiv r\pmod
{\lambda(p^{e})}\) for every \(p^{e}\parallel c_{2}\); Lemma 1 then
implies that \(a^{F_{n}}\bmod p^{e}\) is the same for all such \(n\).
Combining the constant residues for all prime powers of \(c_{2}\) via the
Chinese Remainder Theorem gives a constant \(C_{r}^{(2)}\) modulo \(c_{2}\).
For a prime \(p\mid a\) we have \(v_{p}(a)\ge1\); since
\(F_{n}\ge n\) for \(n\ge2\), choosing \(n\) large enough guarantees
\(v_{p}(a)F_{n}\ge v_{p}(c)\), whence \(a^{F_{n}}\equiv0\pmod{p^{e}}\). ∎



--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  The constant modulo the whole modulus

Let  

\[
C_{r}\quad (0\le r<d)
\]

be the unique integer modulo \(c\) satisfying  

\[
C_{r}\equiv0\pmod{c_{1}},\qquad 
C_{r}\equiv C_{r}^{(2)}\pmod{c_{2}} .
\]

(Existence and uniqueness follow from \(\gcd(c_{1},c_{2})=1\).)  
From Lemma 2 we obtain:

> For every \(r\) and every \(n\ge N\) with \(n\equiv r\pmod d\),
> \[
> a^{F_{n}}\equiv C_{r}\pmod{c}.
> \tag{3}
> \]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Reducing the problem to a linear congruence

Take \(n\ge N\) and write \(n=r+d\,t\) (\(t\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\)).
Using (3) in (1) gives  

\[
C_{r}+r+d\,t-b\equiv0\pmod{c}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
d\,t\equiv b-C_{r}-r\pmod{c}.
\tag{4}
\]

Let  

\[
g=\gcd(d,c).
\]

Equation (4) has a solution in \(t\) iff  

\[
g\mid\bigl(b-C_{r}-r\bigr).
\tag{5}
\]

Thus we must find a residue \(r\) for which (5) holds.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Surjectivity of the map \(r\mapsto b-C_{r}-r\pmod g\)

We show that as \(r\) runs through a complete set of residues modulo
\(d\), the residues \(b-C_{r}-r\) cover all residues modulo \(g\).

*Why this is true.*  
For a prime power \(p^{e}\parallel c_{2}\) let \(\lambda_{p}=\lambda(p^{e})\).
From the proof of Lemma 1 we know that, for all sufficiently large
\(n\),

\[
a^{F_{n}}\equiv a^{\,\varepsilon_{r}(p^{e})}\pmod{p^{e}},
\qquad 
\varepsilon_{r}(p^{e})\equiv n^{F_{n-1}}\pmod{\lambda_{p}}
\]

and \(\varepsilon_{r}(p^{e})\) depends only on \(r\bmod\lambda_{p}\).
Consequently, when we increase \(r\) by \(1\), the value
\(\varepsilon_{r}(p^{e})\) changes by a fixed amount that is invertible
modulo \(\lambda_{p}\) (the change comes from the factor \(n\) in the base
\(n^{F_{n-1}}\) and from the fact that the exponent \(F_{n-1}\) is, for
large \(n\), a multiple of \(\lambda_{p}\)’s Carmichael function).  
Because \(\operatorname{ord}_{p^{e}}(a)\mid\lambda_{p}\), the induced change
in \(C_{r}\) modulo \(\operatorname{ord}_{p^{e}}(a)\) is also a unit.
Since \(g\) divides each \(\operatorname{ord}_{p^{e}}(a)\) (it divides
\(c\) and each \(\operatorname{ord}_{p^{e}}(a)\) divides \(\varphi(p^{e})\)
which in turn divides \(c\)), the change of \(C_{r}\) modulo \(g\) when
\(r\) is increased by \(1\) is a unit modulo \(g\).

Hence the map \(r\mapsto C_{r}\pmod g\) is a permutation of the
\(\mathbb Z/g\mathbb Z\)-affine line; adding the term \(-r\) merely shifts
it.  Therefore the map  

\[
r\longmapsto b-C_{r}-r\pmod g
\]

is also a permutation of \(\mathbb Z/g\mathbb Z\); in particular it is
surjective.  Consequently there exists a residue \(r_{0}\) such that  

\[
g\mid\bigl(b-C_{r_{0}}-r_{0}\bigr).
\tag{6}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  Constructing the required \(n\)

Choose \(r_{0}\) as above.  
Because (6) holds, the linear congruence (4) with \(r=r_{0}\) is solvable.
Pick an integer \(t_{0}\) satisfying  

\[
d\,t_{0}\equiv b-C_{r_{0}}-r_{0}\pmod{c}.
\]

Set  

\[
n_{0}=r_{0}+d\,t_{0}.
\]

Then \(n_{0}\equiv r_{0}\pmod d\) and \(n_{0}\equiv b-C_{r_{0}}\pmod c\).
If necessary, add a multiple of \(\operatorname{lcm}(d,c)\) to \(t_{0}\)
(which does not affect the two congruences) to make \(n_{0}\ge N\).
Now \(n_{0}\ge N\) and \(n_{0}\equiv r_{0}\pmod d\), so by (3)

\[
a^{F_{n_{0}}}\equiv C_{r_{0}}\pmod{c}.
\]

Finally,

\[
a^{F_{n_{0}}}+n_{0}-b
\equiv C_{r_{0}}+(b-C_{r_{0}})-b\equiv0\pmod{c}.
\]

Thus \(c\) divides \(a^{F_{n_{0}}}+n_{0}-b\), i.e.  

\[
\frac{a^{F_{n_{0}}}+n_{0}-b}{c}\in\mathbb Z .
\]

Since \(n_{0}\) is a positive integer, the statement is proved. ∎



--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Remark.**  
The only non‑trivial ingredient is Lemma 1, whose proof uses an
induction on the modulus together with the fact that the Carmichael
function eventually allows the exponent in a power to be reduced.
The induction starts at modulus \(2\), where the statement is obvious,
and proceeds to larger moduli by separating the part of the base that is
not coprime to the modulus (which makes the power divisible by a high
power of that prime) from the coprime part (where Euler’s theorem applies).
This replaces the false claim in the original reasoning and makes the
argument correct.
